title: Why Critical Thinking Starts With Something We Were Told to Stop Doing
author: Eva Keiffenheim
summary: Eva Keiffenheim recounts losing a graduate seminar debate to a classmate who had memorized the facts while she frantically searched online, and uses it to argue that memory and understanding are not rivals. Drawing on working memory limits and sources such as Michelle Miller and Make It Stick, she explains that familiar knowledge frees attention for connections and argument. She gives three reasons long-term memory shapes thinking: prior knowledge gives new facts something to attach to, critical thinking requires technical fluency, and active retrieval locks learning in. Her practical rule is to internalize the foundational ideas you think with and leave fleeting details to notes.
points: Working memory is limited, so looking up basic terms mid-argument drains the capacity needed for complex thinking.
Prior knowledge gives new information a framework to attach to, so experts and novices reading the same document literally see different things.
Critical thinking without technical knowledge gives people little guidance on where to start challenging a claim.
Retrieval practice and explaining ideas in your own words reveal gaps that rereading hides.
Remember the core ideas you think with and look up fleeting details such as schedules or rarely used syntax.
quotes: Working memory—the information we actively hold at any moment—has its limits. When you stop to look up a basic term, date, or concept, you drain that limited space.
Familiar knowledge lets us recognize meaningful patterns instead of processing every detail separately. That leaves more capacity for making connections and following an argument.
Knowledge works like roots in soil. Bare earth washes away in the rain, but soil woven with roots drinks the water in and holds it.
Yet encouraging critical thinking without teaching the underlying facts gives people little guidance on how to begin.
Skimming a text gives you a warm feeling of familiarity. You nod along, feeling informed.
Calling an idea back from memory makes it easier to retrieve later. Explaining the connections between ideas gives you practice using the knowledge you want to keep.
As a rule of thumb, remember the core ideas you need to think with. Look up fleeting or changing details.

Knowledge in long-term memory lets us work around the limitations of working memory. Facts do not merely give us something to think about: having them readily available changes how effectively we can think.
